# 20260901

## Summary

Replaced the paper's methodology (previously a Mundlak correlated-random-effects
regression) with an interactive fixed-effects model (@Bai2009) on
cohort-percentile citations, benchmarked against a simpler additive
two-way fixed-effects alternative via out-of-sample cross-validation. Built
and verified the full supporting code pipeline (`data/04_interactive_fixed_effects/code/02`–`09`),
reframed the paper around its central finding, and pushed the project to
GitHub.

## What was done

- Rebuilt `draft.qmd`'s Statistical Methods, Empirical Strategy, and
  Results sections around the interactive/additive fixed-effects model
  (`02_ife_cohort_percentile.R`, `05_additive_fe_pctile.R`), selected via
  out-of-sample CV (`06_model_comparison_cv.R`): both specifications tie
  at $R^2=0.132$ out-of-sample, so the additive model is adopted as
  primary for its simplicity.
- Verified the additive model against a placebo (randomly permuted
  outcomes): real out-of-sample $R^2=0.132$ vs. placebo $R^2=-0.132$,
  confirming genuine signal rather than overfitting.
- Compared pre/post-1992 T6-entry cohorts (`04_cohort_compare_1992.R`,
  `07_cohort_heterogeneity.R`): human-capital dispersion is significantly
  wider post-1992, concentrated among large-team collaborators, but a
  direct interaction test finds no increased *return* to team size.
- Ran a calendar-year structural-break scan (`08_structural_break_scan.R`)
  on $\gamma_y$: found a strong break at 1983 (unrelated to ICT; likely a
  Scopus coverage artifact), no comparable break in the 1991–2000
  ICT-diffusion window.
- **Key finding**: a peer-environment design (`09_peer_effects.R`)
  comparing actual coauthors to co-located-but-never-coauthored
  researchers shows the apparent benefit of a strong early-career peer
  pool is a between-institution artifact — within institution, an
  unusually strong contemporaneous peer cohort predicts *worse* long-run
  performance (congestion, not spillover). This became the paper's
  central result; retitled to *"Ability or Environment? Peer Congestion
  in the Making of Academic Human Capital"* and reordered the
  introduction/literature review/discussion accordingly.
- Softened several abstract/results sentences that had overstated the
  returns-channel null result (a level-shock test and a team-size-return
  test do not, on their own, rule out a general redistributive ability
  premium).
- Cleaned up the repo: archived-then-deleted two unused analysis scripts
  and their outputs, removed an orphaned OpenAlex-sourced CSV and two
  stray folders, relocated `deep_impact_journal_list.qmd` into
  `data/02_publication_history/input/`.
- Initialized git, rewrote `.gitignore` (all data, all PDFs, `.venv/`,
  `.claude/` excluded; `.gitkeep` placeholders keep the folder layout
  visible), and pushed to
  [github.com/JayLeeRes/human-capital-tech-progress](https://github.com/JayLeeRes/human-capital-tech-progress)
  (public).

## Open questions for next time

- The paper's returns-channel tests (level shock, team-size return) do
  not directly test whether the ability premium changed for *incumbents*
  specifically (a $\hat\psi_i$-style pre/post comparison, as in the
  original Mundlak draft, would be more direct). Not yet rebuilt in the
  current framework.
- $\lambda_{i2}$ (the second interactive-model factor, $r=2$) does not
  correlate with any of the covariates tried so far (team size, career
  length, author's own mean observed age); its substantive meaning is
  still unresolved.
